title: The ‘tragedy of the commons’ often isn’t a tragedy at all
body: In 1968 ecologist Garrett Hardin argued that when a pasture is open to every herder, each one gains by adding another cow, keeping all of its milk while the lost grass is shared by everyone, so the pasture gets ruined. The idea has been applied to overfishing and pollution. But Elinor Ostrom and others found the tragedy less common and easier to solve than Hardin claimed: the users of real pastures, forests, fisheries and irrigation systems have often made rules of their own that kept them going. In 2009 that work made her the first woman to win the economics Nobel.

slides.alt: Flat illustrated animation of a fenced common pasture with four farms. In a simple model, every herder adds a cow each season until the grass turns to bare earth; then the herders follow their own rules, three cows per farm, and the pasture stays green.

slides.heading: Where the idea began
slides.text: Hardin built on an 1833 pamphlet by the English economist William Forster Lloyd, who imagined herders overgrazing a shared village pasture. Aristotle had made a similar point.

slides.heading: Ostrom’s design principles
slides.text: The long-lasting commons she studied tended to share features: clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions that users can help change, monitors answerable to the users, graduated penalties and cheap ways to settle disputes.

slides.heading: Real examples
slides.text: Her book Governing the Commons drew on irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines, mountain villages in Switzerland and Japan, and fisheries in Nova Scotia and Indonesia. One Swiss alpine commons has been run by its farmers since 1517.

slides.question: Which is one of the features Ostrom found in lasting commons?
options: A single owner for the resource
slides.explanation: Lasting commons tend to have clear boundaries, rules the users can help change, monitoring, graduated penalties and cheap ways to settle disputes.

slides.heading: Match the thinker to the work
slides.explanation: Hardin built on Lloyd’s pamphlet; Ostrom’s studies of real commons made her the first woman to win the economics Nobel.

slides.heading: Hardin’s second thoughts
slides.text: Because his use of “commons” was so often misunderstood, Hardin later remarked that he should have called his essay “The Tragedy of the Unregulated Commons”.
